query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings, the wear performance is primarily governed by the in-situ formation of a stable, protective oxide tribolayer that forms when a reactive element (such as Cr or Al) exceeds a critical concentration in the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating with a base composition that has a reactive element content below the critical threshold needed for optimal tribolayer formation.
generation.intervention: Systematic increase in the reactive element content (e.g., Cr or Al) in the alloy composition to span values below and above the threshold.
generation.conditions: Conduct pin‐on‐disk wear tests at ambient temperature under a controlled load and sliding speed; post-test surface analyses (SEM/EDS, XPS) are performed to assess tribolayer (oxide) formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The in-situ formed oxide tribolayer on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: A higher content of the reactive element promotes tribo-oxidation during sliding, leading to rapid formation and stabilization of a protective oxide layer. This tribolayer acts as a lubricant and barrier against direct metal-to-metal contact, thus reducing wear rate and friction coefficient. Coatings below the threshold fail to form a continuous protective layer, resulting in poorer wear performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: When the reactive element concentration exceeds the critical threshold, a stable oxide tribolayer will form on the wear track, correlating with a measurable drop in wear rate and friction coefficient compared to coatings with lower reactive element content.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy coatings with reactive element content below the critical threshold exhibit minimal tribolayer formation, leading to higher wear rates and friction coefficients.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under ambient temperature conditions with fixed load and sliding speed. Its relevance at elevated temperatures or under drastically different sliding conditions remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold value for the reactive element and the quantitative magnitude of wear performance improvement are not precisely determined and may vary with the testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of HEA coatings with systematically varied reactive element (e.g., Cr or Al) contents that span values below and above the anticipated threshold. Subject all coatings to identical pin‐on‐disk wear tests under controlled load, sliding speed, and ambient temperature conditions. After the tests, analyze the worn surfaces using SEM/EDS and XPS to detect and characterize the oxide tribolayer.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and composition (via XPS/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the reactive element content does not result in a clear transition in wear performance (i.e., no significant reduction in wear rate or friction coefficient) and the protective oxide tribolayer is not observed to form on the worn surfaces above a certain reactive element concentration, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This uncovers that NiX still outperforms Ni3X in resisting the elastic–plastic deformation involved with abrasive wear even at 400 °C. The higher high-temperature hardness of NiX may be responsible for the low wear rate compared to Ni3X at 400 °C (Fig. 3A). Nanoindentation tests (Fig. S2) also show that H on the worn surface of NiX (5.9 GPa) at 400 °C is higher than that of Ni3X (4.9 GPa). In summary, we propose a strategy to design wear-resistant alloys through in-situ formation of strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces during wear, a process which we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. A representative bcc structured (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy was developed, which yields a two orders of magnitude lower wear rate than the reference TiNbZr alloy. Upon wear in ambient air, the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy forms an in-situ 400-nm-thick amorphous-crystalline nanocomposite surface layer, through reaction with the environmental O, comprising an amorphous Ti17Nb13Zr13Fe2O55 matrix containing ~10-nm-sized Ag nanocrystals. The high wear resistance of the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy is achieved by the synergistic effect of the low friction coefficient (~0.09) of the alloy and the in-situ formation of an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface, which exhibits a high strength and homogeneous plastic flow behavior. chosen.why: This move directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that the wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by the in situ formation and stability of a protective tribolayer. By systematically changing the alloy composition to control the availability of a reactive element that promotes oxide formation, the study distinguishes the hypothesis from a baseline by observing a predictable improvement in wear resistance when the tribolayer is optimally formed. The approach uses standard, established wear testing and characterization techniques, making it most plausible and directly relevant to the research question.
